name: How to Design a Kitchen for Wheelchair Users

step.name: Step 1
step.text: Designing a kitchen for wheelchair users involves specific considerations to ensure independence and ease of use. Here’s a step-by-step approach to get it right.

step.name: Step 2
step.text: Step 1: Measure and Plan for Movement. Begin by measuring the user’s turning radius to ensure adequate space for maneuvering. Plan for wider circulation paths, ideally at least 36-42 inches, so a wheelchair can move freely without obstruction. Remember that accessibility changes are much easier to integrate before walls, cabinets, or plumbing are installed.

step.name: Step 3
step.text: Step 2: Adjust Counter Heights and Layout. Consider lowering or splitting counter heights to accommodate seated meal preparation. You might have one section at a standard height and another lower, or even adjustable sections. Place appliances and work zones to minimize transfer distance and overreach. The sink, cooktop, and prep areas all need clear space underneath for seated access.

step.name: Step 4
step.text: Step 3: Choose Accessible Storage Solutions. Avoid relying solely on upper storage that requires overreaching. Instead, opt for pull-out pantry shelves, lower cabinets with pull-down shelving systems, and deep drawers that are easy to access from a seated position. Ensure frequently used items are stored within easy reach, between lap and eye level.

step.name: Step 5
step.text: Step 4: Select User-Friendly Fixtures and Appliances. Install lever-style handles for faucets and doors, as they are easier to operate. Choose appliances with front-mounted controls and side-opening oven doors. Ensure switches and outlets are placed at an accessible height. Don't forget non-slip flooring for safety. If your project involves moving walls or changing plumbing/electrical, compliance and permits may be needed, so a professional can guide you.
